extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor and antitrust lawyers, policymakers, worker advocates, and commenters on the FTC rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and application of the FTC's final rule banning or limiting non-compete clauses, including definitions (worker, person, senior executive), scope, enforcement prohibitions, and the evidentiary/empirical standards the Commission used. Useful for drafting comments, compliance plans, or legal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "non-compete clause" (final rule wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractual term that prevents a worker from seeking or accepting work in the United States with a different person where such work would begin after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition, or that prevents a worker from operating a business in the United States after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that restraints on concurrent employment are not non-competes under the final rule; technical edits were made to capture clauses that prevent future employment beginning after conclusion of the employment that includes the clause; revised phrasing to cover workers hired through staffing agencies or third parties so such clauses are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for restraints on concurrent employment / fixed-term employment contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts that restrain concurrent employment (e.g., fixed-term 'employment for a period' contracts that do not restrain post-employment conduct) are not treated as non-compete clauses under the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule focuses on restraints that operate after the conclusion of employment; concurrent-employment restraints and mere fixed-term employment obligations are outside the non-compete definition if they do not restrain post-employment conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of third-party hiring and staffing arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-compete definition applies to clauses that restrict workers even when they are hired by one party but work for another (e.g., staffing agencies); therefore the rule covers such non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission revised wording from 'worker's employment with the employer' to 'the employment that includes the term or condition' to eliminate ambiguity and prevent evasion through third-party hiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of union no-raid agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: A union no-raid agreement would be covered only if it is a 'term or condition of employment' and prevents a worker from seeking or accepting work or operating a business in the U.S. after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission's understanding is that typical union no-raid agreements are not terms/conditions of employment that prevent seeking or accepting work or operating a business, and thus generally would not be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-application to business-to-business non-competes (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition generally would not apply to non-competes between businesses (e.g., between motor carriers and brokers), though the Commission declines to opine on specific factual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is focused on employment-related non-competes; factual specifics may affect applicability in particular business-to-business arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "person" for the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'person' means any natural person, partnership, corporation, association, or other legal entity within the Commission's jurisdiction, including any person acting under color or authority of State law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This adopts the statutory definition with the added phrase 'within the Commission's jurisdiction' to clarify the scope of entities subject to the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final definition of "worker" (scope and key revisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'worker' is a natural person who works or who previously worked, without regard to the worker's title or the worker's status under any other State or Federal laws. The non-exhaustive list includes employee, independent contractor, extern, intern, volunteer, apprentice, sole proprietor, and a natural person who works for a franchisee or franchisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three main revisions: (1) expressly includes former workers ('or who previously worked'); (2) removes the phrase 'for an employer' to cover indirect employment arrangements; (3) adds 'without regard to the worker's title or status under any other State or Federal laws' to preclude evasion based on classification or title. The Commission declined to exclude independent contractors or adopt the 'ABC' test, citing misclassification concerns and lack of evidence that such workers are less harmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of independent contractors and sole proprietors as "workers"
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent contractors and sole proprietors are included within the definition of 'worker' and thus within the rule's coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission rejected requests to exclude bona fide independent contractors or sole proprietors, finding insufficient evidence that non-competes affecting them are less harmful and expressing concern that exclusion would incentivize employer misclassification and fail to protect vulnerable workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of franchisee / franchisor relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition states that a franchisee—in the context of a franchisee-franchisor relationship—was proposed to be excluded as a 'worker,' but the final definition includes 'a natural person who works for the franchisee or franchisor' and declines to adopt a categorical exclusion for franchisees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission moved and removed language to avoid implying that only franchisor-franchisee non-competes remain subject to antitrust law; it also recognized commenters' concerns that excluding franchisees could enable evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential treatment for senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adopts a different approach for 'senior executives': existing non-competes entered into before the effective date can remain in force; the rule does not cover those existing agreements. However, entering into or enforcing new non-competes with senior executives after the effective date is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: harms from senior-executive non-competes are characterized principally as tending to negatively affect competitive conditions (restrictive/exclusionary) rather than being exploitative/coercive; practical concerns about extinguishing existing contracts led to grandfathering existing senior-executive non-competes but banning new ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on new non-competes with all workers (effective date rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an unfair method of competition (and a violation of Section 5) for employers to enter into non-competes with workers on or after the final rule's effective date — a comprehensive ban on new non-competes with all workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule specifically prohibits entering into such clauses on or after the effective date; for non-senior executives it also addresses existing agreements differently (see other metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of existing non-competes for non-senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing non-competes entered into before the final rule's effective date that cover workers who are not senior executives are no longer enforceable after the final rule's effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must provide affected non-senior-executive workers with notice that their existing non-competes will not be enforced after the effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited acts defined (enter, enforce, represent)
rubrics_metrics.description: For workers who are not senior executives, it is an unfair method of competition to: enter into or attempt to enter into a non-compete clause; enforce or attempt to enforce a non-compete clause; or represent to the worker that the worker is subject to a non-compete clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For senior executives, similar prohibitions apply only to non-competes entered into after the effective date; the Commission distinguishes enforcement/applicability depending on timing and worker category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 analytical framework for unfair methods of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 5, the Commission assesses (1) whether the conduct is a 'method of competition' (specific conduct vs. a condition of the marketplace), and (2) whether it is 'unfair' meaning it goes beyond competition on the merits. The 'unfair' inquiry has two components: (a) indicia of unfairness, and (b) whether the conduct tends to negatively affect competitive conditions. These components are weighed on a sliding scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal standard requires only a 'tendency' to negatively affect competitive conditions; the inquiry does not require proof that conduct caused actual harm in a specific instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of unfairness: restrictive and exclusionary conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that restricts competitive activity (e.g., preventing a worker from seeking or accepting other work or starting a business, or preventing competitors from hiring that worker) is an indicium of unfairness under Section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-competes are facially restrictive/exclusionary because of their nature and function; this supports finding them unfair when coupled with a tendency to negatively affect competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of unfairness: exploitative and coercive conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that exploits or coerces workers (e.g., by leveraging bargaining power to impose restrictive terms) is an indicium of unfairness under Section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds non-competes for non-senior executives are exploitative and coercive as well as restrictive; for senior executives the Commission did not find evidence of exploitative/coercive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence weighting principle 1: studies of legal-status or enforceability changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more weight to studies examining the effects of a change in legal status or a change in the enforceability of non-competes (before-and-after designs) rather than studies that simply compare workers with and without non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such designs better support causal inference because they reduce confounding; 'use' studies comparing workers with vs without non-competes are less reliable for causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence weighting principle 2: prefer enforceability-change over cross-sectional enforceability comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more weight to studies examining changes in enforceability over time within jurisdictions than to cross-sectional comparisons between States with different enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-sectional comparisons can be polluted by other state-level differences (e.g., cost of living); within-state changes better isolate effects of non-compete enforceability changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence weighting principle 3: multi-state analyses favored
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more weight to studies that assess changes in enforceability across multiple States rather than single-State analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-state analyses reduce the risk that observed outcomes are driven by idiosyncratic factors unique to one State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence weighting principle 4: nuanced, multidimensional measures of enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more weight to studies that use sophisticated, nuanced measures of enforceability (non-binary measures capturing geographic scope, duration, employer burden of proof, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforceability varies along multiple dimensions; binary scales miss important nuance. Multidimensional scales yield greater accuracy and granularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence weighting principle 5: outcome relevance and proxy quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more weight to studies where the outcome studied matches the Commission's outcomes of interest or is an effective proxy; give less weight to studies that use weak or inapt proxies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, patent counts are a weaker proxy for innovation than measures that incorporate patent quality; earnings data at State level are good for earnings but other outcomes may lack direct measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic assessment of empirical studies (additional quality factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the five guiding principles, the Commission's assessment considers overall study characteristics such as data quality, statistical precision, and other context-specific factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission applies expertise to weigh studies holistically rather than mechanically applying the five principles alone; it cites additional studies only when they confirm or check analyses in the NPRM.
